answer: The barn now standing at Combe Farm is not, in CRM terms, the same E22 Human-Made Object as the barn recorded in the 1839 tithe survey -- it is a new E22 that results from a documented transformation of the old one. Model two distinct E22 instances: 'threshing barn at Hollow Farm (pre-1839-1938)' and 'barn at Combe Farm (1938-)', and link them through a single E81 Transformation event: the Hollow Farm barn is what P124 transformed, the Combe Farm barn is what P123 resulted in. This is exactly the pattern the CRM's own scope notes point to: E81's scope note lists 'reconstructions and repurposing of historical buildings or ruins' as a characteristic case, and E11 Modification's own scope note carves this out explicitly -- 'An event should also be documented using an instance of E81 Transformation if it results in the destruction of one or more objects and the simultaneous production of others using parts or material from the originals. In this case, the new items have separate identities.' That matches the case precisely: the frame was dismantled (destruction of the object as it stood), 70% of the oak reused but the roof covering, plinth walls and one whole bay replaced, and the result re-erected four miles away (production of a new object using material from the old). A 2025-12 SIG discussion (unresolved, but consistent with the standing text) uses the closest real analogue -- the Temple of Abu Simbel -- for exactly this reasoning: 'If moving requires separating at substantially new boundaries, such as the Temple of Abu Simbel when it was moved, a new instance of E18 Physical Object is created that incorporates the previous item. The latter process may be documented by the class E81 Transformation.' Simple relocation (E9 Move) does not apply, because E9 presupposes the object keeps its own boundaries intact through the move -- it was not lifted and set down, it was taken apart. Plain E11 Modification/part-replacement (E79/E80) does not apply either, because that presumes continuity of identity through the change, and a 2019 SIG exchange on the ship-of-Theseus problem (Issue 369 thread) draws exactly this line: gradual in-place part replacement can leave identity intact, but full dismantling and later reassembly breaks it -- 'I propose to regard the "reconstructed" as a new E19 object, because the continuity of functionality is broken.' Note also the officially decided Issue 404 outcome: a change of use alone (even for buildings) does not trigger E81 -- but this case is not merely a change of use, it is substantial, documented material replacement plus full dismantle/rebuild, which is exactly what the scope note requires to justify a new object. For the record: the 1839 tithe survey is an E31 Document that P70 documents the Hollow Farm E22; the estate plaque at Combe Farm is evidence of the P124/P123 linkage and can be modelled as an E34 Inscription borne by the Combe Farm E22, itself citable as documentary evidence for the E81 event connecting the two objects.

rejected_alternatives.option: E9 Move (treat Combe Farm barn as the Hollow Farm barn relocated)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E9 Move's scope note (E18/E19 concept dossier and the 2025-12 SIG thread t1874) presupposes the object's own physical boundaries stay intact through the move; Martin Doerr's own gloss is that when 'moving requires separating at substantially new boundaries... a new instance of E18 Physical Object is created' and the process is E81, not E9. The barn was dismantled into components, not moved as a coherent whole.

rejected_alternatives.option: E11 Modification / E79 Part Addition + E80 Part Removal (treat it as the same barn, repaired)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E11's own scope note explicitly excludes this case: when destruction of the old object and production of a new one from its parts/material happen together, 'the new items have separate identities' and E81 is required instead. The 2019 Issue-369 thread (t1170) draws the same line for the ship-of-Theseus case: gradual in-place part swaps preserve identity, but full dismantle-and-reassemble breaks 'continuity of functionality' and yields a new object.

rejected_alternatives.option: No transformation at all -- just record it as the same building because of the plaque and 70% original fabric
rejected_alternatives.why_not: The officially closed Issue 404 clarifies that for buildings a mere change of use does not trigger E81, which could invite treating high material continuity as decisive; but the case is not a mere-use change, and the CRM's own decided text ties the new-object judgement to whether the destruction/production was substantial and simultaneous, which it was here (roof, plinth, and a whole bay replaced, plus full relocation).

notes: Strong support from the current, decided scope notes of E81 and E11, from the closed Issue 404 and Issue 12 outcomes, and from a 2019 mailing-list exchange (t1170) that works through the ship-of-Theseus problem for E19 identity. The single most on-point analogy (Temple of Abu Simbel, dismantled and reassembled) comes from thread t1874, which is a live, unresolved 2025-12 discussion about clarifying E18/E24 movability -- it is Martin Doerr's own proposed scope-note language, not yet ratified, so I flagged it as such rather than as settled doctrine. Nothing in the tools directly addresses vernacular/heritage buildings moved to open-air museums as a named case, so the mapping from the barn onto the Abu Simbel/ship-of-Theseus reasoning is my own inference, not a literal precedent.
